glossary.short: A score from 1 to 9 for how proven a technology is: 1 is an idea on paper, 9 has flown in space many times.
Orbits between about 200 and 2,000 km above the Earth, where most Earth-watching satellites fly.

learnMore.label: NASA Earth Observatory: Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

glossary.short: How high the satellite flies above the ground; lower gives sharper images but more air drag.

learnMore.label: NASA Earth Observatory: Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

glossary.short: A near-polar orbit that passes over each place at the same local time every day, so the lighting is always similar.

learnMore.label: NASA Earth Observatory: Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits

glossary.short: An orbit that passes over both poles, so the satellite sees the whole Earth as it turns underneath.
The tilt of the orbit compared with the equator: 0° circles the equator, 90° passes over the poles.
The time for one trip around the Earth; about 95 minutes in low Earth orbit.
Thin air at the top of the atmosphere slowly drags a satellite down until it burns up; lower orbits decay faster.
How long the satellite keeps working in orbit before it re-enters, runs out of fuel or wears out.
How often the satellite passes over the same place; a fire watch needs at least one look per day.
The width of the strip of ground the instrument sees on each pass; a wider swath means more frequent revisits.
The angle the instrument can see at once; a wide angle gives a wide swath but less detail.
The size on the ground of one image pixel; smaller means sharper images.
The part of each orbit spent in the Earth's shadow, when solar panels produce no power and the battery takes over.
Turns sunlight into electricity for the satellite; more panels give more power but add mass and cost.
Stores energy from the solar panels so the satellite keeps working during eclipse.
The satellite's brain: it runs commands, stores data and keeps every part working together.
The system that measures and turns the satellite's orientation so cameras point at the ground and panels at the Sun.
Thrusters that change the orbit, for example to dodge debris or to stay up longer against air drag.
Sending data from the satellite down to a ground station.
How fast a radio can send data, in megabits per second; higher rates move more data in each short contact.
An antenna on Earth that talks to the satellite while it passes overhead.
The minutes per day a satellite is in view of a ground station and can send data.
A small, standard-sized satellite built from 10 cm cubes called units (U); 6U is six cubes.
A satellite up to a few hundred kilograms: bigger and more capable than a CubeSat, but slower and dearer to build.

learnMore.label: NASA State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology

glossary.short: The rocket that carries the satellite to orbit; each one can lift a certain mass to a given orbit.
Sharing a rocket with many other satellites: cheap, but you go to the orbit the rocket was already flying to.
The share of a rocket's past launches that worked; a lower rate means a higher chance of losing the satellite.
The instruments that do the mission's science, as opposed to the parts that keep the satellite alive.
Light we feel as heat; a thermal camera sees fires by their heat, even at night.
Infrared light just beyond what eyes see, in which hot fires shine very brightly, even through thin smoke.
Spare capacity kept on purpose (mass, power, time, money) so surprises do not break the mission.
Carrying a backup of an important part, so the mission continues if one fails.
A protective state where the satellite switches off non-essential parts and waits for instructions from the ground.
How well a part withstands the charged particles of space, which can upset or damage electronics.
The share of the mission budget each role may spend; moving money between roles needs a request.
What the engineering team costs for every month of development or waiting, paid from the budget.
The date the satellite must be ready; for Wildfire Watch it is the next fire season.
A number that decides which random events happen; the same seed gives the same events, so you can compare designs fairly.

tour.title: Your mission
tour.text: This card tells you what to achieve. Meet all four requirements, R1 to R4, within the budget and before the deadline.

tour.title: Four roles
tour.text: Launch, Spacecraft, Ground and Science each own part of the design and part of the budget. Switch between them with the role tabs.

tour.title: The dashboard
tour.text: Mass, power, budget and the ready-for-launch date update with every choice. Red means a limit is broken.

tour.title: Make a choice
tour.text: Pick a part to see its effect, such as +2 kg, +8 W, +$0.4M or +3 months. Locked options tell you why they are locked.

tour.title: Ask for help
tour.text: Need more power, mass or money than your role has? Open a request or offer a trade to another role.

tour.title: Approve and launch
tour.text: When the design looks ready, approve it and launch. Events will test your margins, and the report explains what happened and why.

advisorLines.text: I pick the rocket and the orbit. A rideshare is cheap, but it only goes to 525 km sun-synchronous.
The satellite is heavier than this rocket can lift to our orbit. We need a lighter design or a bigger rocket.
At this altitude the orbit decays in under a year. Let's fly higher or add propulsion.
This rocket has a short track record. It saves money, but we could lose everything at launch.
I build the satellite itself and provide the power everyone else uses.
We draw more power than the panels make. I can add panels, but that costs mass and money.
This part has not flown yet. It performs better, but it adds months and risk.
We are close to the fire-season deadline. One more delay and we wait a whole year.
I get the data down to Earth: radios, ground stations and contact time.
We cannot downlink 1 GB a day. Another ground station or a faster radio would fix it.
A faster radio needs about 10 W more. Can Spacecraft provide it?
I choose the instruments and track the science requirements.
We don't see the region every day. A wider-angle instrument or a higher orbit would help.
Our camera can't see active fires. We need an infrared instrument.
A thermal camera would let us see fires at night, for extra science. It needs more power and budget.
My area is over its budget allocation. I need to ask another role for money, or choose cheaper parts.
All four requirements are met. Check the margins, then we can approve the design.
